analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover COVID-19 treatments free of charge during the pandemic emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2020 with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans to include every drug approved or FDA-authorized to treat COVID-19 on their formularies for the duration of the declared public health emergency, to charge seniors no deductible, copayment, or coinsurance for those drugs, and to skip prior-authorization and other utilization controls (except safety-based quantity limits) [S2, S3]. In practice, a senior on Medicare who got a COVID-19 treatment would have walked out of the pharmacy paying nothing. The cost would have fallen on the insurance plans that provide Medicare drug coverage. The bill was introduced on May 8, 2020, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, and never taken up by either one; it drew no cosponsors and received no vote before the Congress ended [S1, S4, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 40 million seniors and disabled people enrolled in Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans would pay nothing out of pocket for COVID-19 treatments — a meaningful protection during a pandemic that fell hardest on older people. Drug manufacturers would also benefit from a guaranteed, unrestricted market, since every plan would have to cover their COVID-19 drugs with no utilization controls.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans would have to include every approved or FDA-authorized COVID-19 treatment on their formularies for the duration of the public health emergency.
Plans could not charge seniors any deductible, copayment, or coinsurance for those drugs, so treatment would be free at the pharmacy for roughly the duration of the declared emergency.
Plans could not use prior authorization or other utilization controls (beyond safety-based quantity limits) to delay or restrict access to COVID-19 treatments.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers would bear the cost of providing COVID-19 drugs free of charge, since the bill set no federal payment to offset the lost cost-sharing; that cost could eventually show up in the premiums seniors pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill was an open-ended mandate on insurance plans: it required every Medicare drug plan and Medicare Advantage plan to cover all marketed and authorized COVID-19 treatments with no deductibles, copayments, or prior authorization for as long as the public health emergency lasted, with no estimate of what that would cost plans or how it might affect the premiums seniors pay.

It barred prior authorization and other utilization controls (except quantity limits for safety), so plans and ultimately Medicare could not steer patients to cheaper or better-supplied options or manage spending on very expensive authorized drugs.
The bill was written in May 2020, before any COVID-19 treatment had been approved or authorized, so Congress had no way to know which drugs, or what total spending, the mandate would cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real but time-limited: free Medicare coverage of COVID-19 treatments would have removed a cost barrier for seniors during a deadly pandemic, which is exactly when cost barriers matter most. The cost was an open-ended federal mandate on drug plans, which could feed back into higher Medicare premiums; the bill also placed no limits on what plans would pay for authorized drugs. On balance, the help to seniors during the emergency likely outweighed those costs, but the bill was never debated, so no one weighed the trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced it, both committees it was sent to never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Casten introduced the bill on May 8, 2020, during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day; neither committee ever acted on it.
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor at any point.
The bill's only actions were its introduction and referral; it never received a hearing or a vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare drug plans and insurers are better off, because they were never required to cover COVID-19 treatments without cost-sharing; seniors gained nothing because the bill died without a vote.

for.name: Sean Casten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 8, 2020, requiring Medicare drug plans to cover COVID-19 treatments without cost-sharing.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 8, 2020 and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out.

against.what_they_did: Chaired the primary committee of referral and never scheduled consideration of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan line ever formed around it.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: The bill would have required these plans to cover all marketed and authorized COVID-19 drugs with no cost-sharing and no prior authorization, shifting the full cost of treatments onto the plans during the emergency, which could later flow back into premiums. As written, it set no offset for plans.

Any drug approved or authorized to treat COVID-19 would have to be placed on every Medicare drug plan's formulary without utilization management, guaranteeing a large insured market with no payer pushback during the emergency. The bill imposed no price limits on those drugs.
Filling prescriptions with no copayment and no prior authorization removes dispensing friction and payment barriers for high-volume COVID-19 treatments.
